ideas.title: Don't Run to Him
ideas.premise: When my brother broke through the ice twenty meters from me at blue hour, I had a phone, my voice and about ten minutes before his arms gave out, and every step toward the hole could have put us both in the water.
ideas.hook: If your brother falls through the ice, don't run to him.
ideas.twist: The instinct is to sprint to the hole and grab him, and that's how one victim becomes two. The ice that just broke under him is the weakest ice on the lake. What to do: stop, call 911, then talk him through it from a safe spot (calm the breathing, turn back the way he came, arms on the ice, kick flat, slide out and roll away). Only reach for him lying flat, never standing at the edge. 'Talk, call, reach, don't go.'
ideas.world: A sequel that swaps roles: this time the brother falls in and Eli is the rescuer. Sunset walk between the shacks, then the crack at blue hour by the red shack. SIDE view for the fall and Eli's freeze-frame choice: the red dashed ghost runs to the hole, and the real Eli stops and drops flat. CUT view shows the brother's trapped jacket air and arms on the ice. TOP map shows the two paths, the ghost's straight run onto weak ice versus the real Eli's stop point. Speech bubbles carry the coaching. Night falls as the brother rolls clear. Brother-distance pill: 20 m, then the ghost's 0 m flashing red, then holding at 8 m.
diagrams: TOP map: the red dashed 'mistake' path straight to the hole vs Eli's stop point, with the ring of weak ice marked around the hole
1-10-1 card with the phase strip moving: 1 min breathe, 10 min to self-rescue
911-call card: 'lake name, which shore, nearest shack, how many in the water'
CUT cross-section: brother's arms on the ice, legs kicking flat, callout 'turn back the way you came, that ice held you'
Brother-distance pill plus angle meter callout: 'lie flat, spread your weight'
ideas.fact: Minnesota DNR ice-safety guidance: if someone falls through, call 911 and don't go out to them; reach or throw something from a safe spot. 1-10-1 principle (Dr. Gordon Giesbrecht, cold-water physiologist): about 1 minute of cold shock, about 10 minutes of useful movement, up to about 1 hour before hypothermia causes unconsciousness.
ideas.verify: Exact current Minnesota DNR wording for helping someone who fell through ice (call 911, reach/throw, don't go). The 1-10-1 figures and how they are attributed (Giesbrecht / Cold Water Boot Camp). Whether talking someone through self-rescue is endorsed by DNR or a lifesaving body (Red Cross / Lifesaving Society). Keep any 'rescuers become victims' line as a qualitative claim unless a sourced number is found.
ideas.risk: Low-medium. A rescue scene with a family member, so keep it calm with no near-drowning drama. Never show Eli standing at the hole edge except as the red ghost. Must not suggest untrained people should go out onto the ice.

ideas.title: Follow the Footprints
ideas.premise: At sunset I took a shortcut along a stranger's footprints toward my brother's red shack, with about twenty minutes of light left to read the ice and only my ice picks and the ice under my boots to tell me if it would hold.
ideas.hook: Why you must never trust footprints on a frozen lake.
ideas.twist: Myth: someone walked here, so the ice is safe. Footprints only show that the ice held one person at some earlier moment. Near a creek mouth, moving water thins the ice from below while the top looks the same. Snow-covered white ice is much weaker than clear ice. What to do: when a boot print fills with water or the ice turns dark and slushy, stop, turn around in your own tracks, stay away from inlets, and go the long way.
ideas.world: A prequel to 'Ten Minutes Under': the same creek mouth, but this time Eli stops in time, so the episode ends with no fall. SIDE view at sunset: the footprint trail heading toward the creek mouth. Boot-print close-up as the turn: water seeping into the print. CUT view: the ruler shows thick ice near the shacks and thin ice over the moving current. TOP map at blue hour: the footprint shortcut vs the long safe way along the shacks. The brother waves from the red shack, and the brother-distance pill ticks down along the safe route. Ends at night with Eli safe at the shack, then the PART 2 card.
diagrams: Boot-print close-up: water filling the print, swatch chip 'DARK + SLUSHY = STOP'
CUT cross-section: ice-thickness ruler near the shacks vs over the creek current, with arrows showing water wearing the ice from below
Minnesota DNR ice-thickness ladder (10 cm to walk) with a callout 'white ice: roughly half as strong'
TOP map: the stranger's footprint shortcut through the creek mouth vs Eli's longer safe route
Ice-thickness pill dropping step by step as Eli follows the prints
ideas.fact: Minnesota DNR: at least 10 cm (4 in) of new clear ice to walk on, and white or 'snow' ice is only about half as strong as new clear ice, so double the guideline. DNR also warns that ice is thinner near inlets, outlets and moving water.
ideas.verify: The DNR thickness figures and their metric conversions as shown on the ladder card. The 'white ice is about half as strong' wording. The DNR wording about moving water, inlets and springs. Whether water seeping into boot prints is a recognized warning sign (it is common advice, but get a source).
ideas.risk: Medium for originality, because it uses the same creek mouth as 'Ten Minutes Under'. Present it clearly as the prequel 'how I should have read it' with a new opening shot and a new camera path. Safety risk is low.

ideas.title: The Walk Back
ideas.premise: I had just rolled out of the hole, soaked through, with night coming and the wind rising. My truck was a kilometer away on shore and my brother's red shack was two hundred meters away, and every minute in wet clothes made my hands slower.
ideas.hook: If you climb out of a frozen lake, don't walk home.
ideas.twist: Myth: once you're out of the water, you're safe. The cold keeps working on wet clothes in the wind, and your hands and judgment fail before you notice. What to do: don't stand up next to the hole. Roll and crawl away until you're on proven ice. Then head for the NEAREST shelter, not the car or home. Call 911, get the wet layers off, get dry and warm, and get checked even if you feel fine.
ideas.world: A direct sequel to 'Ten Minutes Under' and a cliffhanger payoff. It opens on Eli rolling away from the hole at blue hour. The freeze-frame shows the red ghost standing up and heading for the far shore, which is the mistake. TOP map: the truck a kilometer away vs the red shack 200 m away. The brother runs out from the shack (runner's path) and the brother-distance pill closes in. The December clock carries the story into night. Snow starts. It ends in the warm glow of the shack.
diagrams: TOP map: distance arrows, truck on shore 1 km vs red shack 200 m, the runner's path for the brother
SIDE view freeze-frame: red dashed ghost standing at the hole edge vs Eli lying flat and rolling, with the angle meter labeled 'stay flat'
1-10-1 card extended: after you're out, the clock keeps running
911-call card plus swatch chips for warning signs: 'shivering · clumsy hands · confusion'
Water-temperature / timer pill switching to an 'out of the water' timer
ideas.fact: CDC: hypothermia warning signs include shivering, exhaustion, confusion, fumbling hands, memory loss, slurred speech and drowsiness, and its first-aid advice is to get the person into a warm room, remove wet clothing and seek medical help. 1-10-1 (Dr. Gordon Giesbrecht): up to about one hour before hypothermia causes unconsciousness.
ideas.verify: The CDC hypothermia signs and its first-aid wording (keep it general with no medical procedures). That 1-10-1's 'one hour' refers to time in the water, so it must not be stated as a time on land. DNR or Coast Guard advice about rolling away from the hole and seeking the nearest shelter.
ideas.risk: Medium. This is close to medical territory. Limit it to widely known CDC first-aid basics (shelter, dry layers, 911, get checked) with no rubbing, drinks or medication talk. It also rests on 'Ten Minutes Under', so new viewers need a one-line recap.

ideas.title: Whiteout on the Ice
ideas.premise: Halfway back to shore at blue hour, a snow squall erased the pines and my own footprints. I had a phone on thirty percent battery and my brother's shack somewhere behind me, and I had to decide whether to walk for shore or stop.
ideas.hook: If a whiteout catches you on the ice, don't walk for shore.
ideas.twist: Myth: just walk straight and you'll hit the shore. Without landmarks, people drift into curves without noticing, and here a curve leads to the thin ice at the creek mouth. What to do: stop the moment you lose the shoreline. Back-track only while your own trail is still visible, or stay put, keep your back to the wind, keep the phone warm inside your jacket, and call 911 with your best location. Your brother's shack is worth more than the shore.
ideas.world: Sunset is clear, then blue hour brings the snow squall with heavy snow particles and a white flash. SIDE view: the pines fade out and the footprint trail fills in. TOP map is the star: the red dashed ghost's 'straight' path bends toward the creek mouth and the hole. The brother in the red shack is a voice on the phone, shown in speech bubbles, and the brother-distance pill shows how close safety really was. Ends at night with the brother's light finding him.
diagrams: TOP map: the 'straight line' Eli thinks he walks vs the real curving path toward the creek mouth
SIDE view: shoreline visibility fading, with a callout 'lost the shore = STOP'
Boot-print close-up: his own prints filling with snow, a countdown tag
911-call card: what to say when you can't see anything (lake, which shacks, last landmark)
Brother-distance pill plus a swatch chip 'phone inside jacket: cold drains batteries'
ideas.fact: Souman et al., 2009 (Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics, published in Current Biology): people walking without a visible sun or landmarks walked in circles. The National Weather Service issues Snow Squall Warnings for sudden whiteout bursts.
ideas.verify: Details of the Souman 2009 walking-in-circles study (conditions, wording, no exaggeration). How the NWS describes snow squalls. Phone makers' guidance on cold and battery drain. Official advice (DNR / NWS) on what to do when caught in a whiteout on the ice: stay put vs back-track.
ideas.risk: Low-medium. 'Stay put' vs 'back-track' advice must match an official source. Snow-heavy frames can hide the characters, so readability needs checking in the storyboard.

ideas.title: The Quiet Shack
ideas.premise: My brother lay down for a nap in his red shack with the heater running, and when he didn't answer the door I had minutes to work out why, get him into the cold air and call 911.
ideas.hook: If your ice shack gives you a headache, don't take a nap.
ideas.twist: Myth: you'd smell it if the heater was a problem. Carbon monoxide has no color or smell, and the first signs feel like flu or simple tiredness: headache, dizziness, sleepiness. What to do: get everyone out into fresh air, call 911, and don't go back in. Every shack with a heater needs a working CO alarm and ventilation.
ideas.world: Only the outside of the shacks is drawn, so the story stays outside the red shack. Sunset arrival, then a speech bubble from the brother ('just a headache, gonna lie down'). At blue hour comes the silence: Eli knocks, opens the door and pulls back. The brother is shown lying down and later sitting up in the snow outside. SIDE view at night: the warm shack glow vs the cold safe air outside. TOP map shows the other shacks and the route the responders take.
diagrams: SIDE view of the red shack with a callout arrow 'CO: no color, no smell' and heater-exhaust arrows
Swatch chips: 'headache · dizzy · sleepy · confused' marked 'not just tired'
911-call card
Freeze-frame paused look: the red ghost going back inside vs Eli staying out in the fresh air
Tag on the shack: 'CO alarm + vent' as STEP 1 / STEP 2 stamps
ideas.fact: CDC: carbon monoxide is an odorless, colorless gas, and the most common symptoms of CO poisoning are headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain and confusion. Minnesota DNR recommends CO detectors and ventilation in fish houses.
ideas.verify: The CDC CO symptom list and its wording. The exact Minnesota DNR guidance on fish-house heaters, ventilation and CO alarms. Make sure no line gives medical treatment beyond 'fresh air + 911'.
ideas.risk: Medium. It touches medical and gas-hazard topics (keep it strictly to CDC basics, with no chemistry or heater-repair talk). The brother is shown unconscious, which is a sensitive image for young viewers. The pack has no shack interior, so it is weaker to show.
